subproblem.title: Integral triangularization from a primitive eigenvector
subproblem.statement: Let γ∈SL₂(ℤ) and ε,p,q∈ℤ. Assume ε²=1, IsCoprime p q, and γ(p,q)ᵀ=(εp,εq)ᵀ. Then there exist σ∈SL₂(ℤ) and b∈ℤ such that the underlying matrix of σ⁻¹γσ is (ε b;0 ε).
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (γ : Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup (Fin 2) ℤ) (ε p q : ℤ), ε ^ 2 = 1 → IsCoprime p q → (γ : Matrix (Fin 2) (Fin 2) ℤ).mulVec ![p, q] = ![ε * p, ε * q] → ∃ (σ : Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup (Fin 2) ℤ) (b : ℤ), (σ⁻¹ * γ * σ : Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup (Fin 2) ℤ).val = Matrix.of ![![ε, b], ![0, ε]]
subproblem.natural_proof:
1. Fix γ∈SL₂(ℤ) and ε,p,q∈ℤ with ε²=1, IsCoprime p q, and γ(p,q)=ε(p,q). By the definition of IsCoprime, choose u,v∈ℤ satisfying up+vq=1.
2. Put r=−v and s=u, and let S=(p r;q s). Its determinant is ps−qr=pu+qv=up+vq=1. Thus S defines an element σ∈SL₂(ℤ), whose inverse has integral entries because it is the adjugate of S.
3. Let δ=σ⁻¹γσ and let e₁=(1,0). Since σe₁=(p,q), the eigenvector hypothesis and associativity of matrix-vector multiplication give δe₁=σ⁻¹γ(p,q)=σ⁻¹(ε(p,q))=εσ⁻¹σe₁=εe₁. Thus the first column of δ is (ε,0).
4. Set b=δ₁₂ and d=δ₂₂, so the underlying integral matrix of δ is (ε b;0 d). As δ∈SL₂(ℤ), its determinant is one. The 2×2 determinant formula therefore gives εd=1.
5. Multiply εd=1 by ε. Since ε²=1, this yields d=ε. Consequently δ=(ε b;0 ε), exactly the matrix represented by Matrix.of ![![ε,b],![0,ε]]. The σ and b already constructed are the required witnesses.
proof_key_steps: Extract Bézout coefficients from IsCoprime p q.
Complete (p,q) to the first column of a determinant-one integral matrix.
Transport the eigenvector equation through conjugation to determine the first column.
Use determinant one and ε²=1 to determine the second diagonal entry.
Return the constructed conjugating matrix and upper-right entry.

Special-linear operations use ordinary matrix multiplication, and Matrix.of correctly represents the displayed matrix. Bézout coefficients produce determinant one; conjugation transports the eigenvector to the first basis vector; determinant one gives εd=1; and ε²=1 gives d=ε. Every step is justified without either child or the parent theorem. The bare name is unreserved. No sibling dependency is needed because the primitive eigenvector is an explicit hypothesis. Together the children give an appropriate acyclic split: the parent applies kernel existence, then triangularization, and finishes using integer powers of T, retaining γ=±I.
